---
title: "Multi-Head Attention"
description: "An attention mechanism that computes several learned attention patterns in parallel and combines them."
term: "Multi-Head Attention"
letter: "M"
category: "Deep Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Multi-head attention lets a model examine relationships between tokens in
several learned ways at once. Each attention head produces a representation,
and the model combines the heads for the next layer.

## Technical explanation

For each head $i$, input representations are projected into queries, keys,
and values. Scaled dot-product attention is:

$$
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
= \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
$$

The outputs of $h$ heads are concatenated and projected:

$$
\operatorname{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)
= \operatorname{Concat}(\operatorname{head}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{head}_h)W^O
$$

Each head has learned projections. Heads are not assigned fixed semantic
roles, even if some heads appear to focus on particular patterns during
analysis.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Multi-head attention is a core component of Transformer models. Parallel
attention patterns help models incorporate contextual relationships across
tokens, supporting language, vision, and multimodal tasks.

## How it works

The model computes attention weights from query-key similarities, uses those
weights to combine value vectors, and repeats this process with different
learned projections for each head. It then concatenates and mixes the head
outputs. Masks can restrict which positions are visible.

and the heads are computed in parallel.

## Practical example

In a sentence such as "The animal sat by the bank," attention can combine
information from different words to help represent context. Multiple heads
provide different learned projections of token relationships, without
guaranteeing that each head has a simple human-readable purpose.

## Common misconceptions

- Heads do not have predefined roles such as "grammar head" or "meaning head."
- More heads do not automatically improve a model; head count is an architecture choice.
- Attention weights are not by themselves a complete explanation of a model's decision.
